Given the entire universe of subjects, I want to tell you about one of my favorite discoveries ever made about human minds: in some languages, you cannot say "to your left."

Guugu Yimithirr, a language spoken in far north Queensland, has no words corresponding to "left" and "right." Direction exists only in absolute terms — north, south, east, west. If you want to warn someone about an insect on their body, you cannot say "there's an ant on your foot." You must say there's an ant on your *southwest* leg.

For a long time, outsiders assumed this was nearly impossible — surely humans lack the internal equipment to track compass directions through ordinary life. But children raised speaking Guugu Yimithirr develop what looks like a sixth sense. Tested deep inside unfamiliar buildings, far from any landmark or glimpse of the sun, they point accurately without hesitation. They weren't born with this. Their language had been rehearsing their attention since infancy, demanding ten thousand tiny daily acts of noticing where they stood relative to the sunrise.

Once you see that languages sculpt perception, you start finding it everywhere. Nearby, speakers of Kuuk Thaayorre arrange pictures of a story unfolding — a man aging, a banana being eaten — laid out from east to west, no matter which way they happen to be sitting when asked. For them, time flows along the compass. Speakers of Tzeltal in Chiapas, Mexico, navigate by the local terrain itself, describing things as "uphill" or "downhill" of wherever they stand, the mountainside stitched permanently into their grammar. And in parts of the Amazon, evidentiality is mandatory: a verb must end with a marker declaring *how you know* — whether you saw it, heard it, inferred it, or were told. In such a language you cannot simply assert. Every sentence is a small signed confession about its own origins.

What delights me about all this is the implication: a language is not really a warehouse for storing observations. It's a set of habits that decides what gets noticed at all. Grammar is a kind of gymnasium, and growing up inside one trains muscles the neighboring gymnasium never develops.

There are roughly seven thousand languages alive right now, and linguists expect a large share of them — perhaps half — to fall silent within a century, mostly not by choice but by erosion. When one goes, it isn't merely a vocabulary lost. It's a hypothesis retired: a working, proof-tested configuration of human attention that our species simply stops running. Ways of holding space, time, and knowledge in mind — configurations that a child in Queensland once grew effortlessly, the way you grew yours — withdrawn from circulation forever.

I find that thought both beautiful and sharp-edged. Beautiful, because it means humanity has already imagined more kinds of minds than any of us will ever occupy alone. Sharp-edged, because the range is narrowing, quietly, every year.

But tonight, somewhere in Hope Vale, there may be someone who says the ant is on the southwest leg — and knows, without pausing to think, exactly which way southwest is. I love that. I love that the world remains stranger than any single language can say.

Let me think about what would actually be good writing here.
